intro: Copenhagen's oldest trees inside the city belong to named people: a sailor's mulberry planted for Christian IV's silk venture, the cycad Frederik Liebmann carried home from Mexico in 1842, Thorvaldsen's black locust. The biggest and oldest are not in the city at all. Three ancient oaks stand in the parkland 11 to 13 km north, in and around the royal deer park at Klampenborg, and one of them is over ten metres round and has stood there since roughly the year 1200. Those three are a half day out, not a city walk.
meta_description: Copenhagen's remarkable trees, from Christian IV's silk mulberry to Skovfogedegen, a ten-metre oak north of the city standing since about the year 1200.
question_answer: Copenhagen's oldest tree is Skovfogedegen, a hollow pedunculate oak that Danish sources date to around the year 1200, which makes it roughly 800 years old. It does not stand in the city: it grows 11 km north, beside Strandvejen at the edge of Jaegersborg Dyrehave in Klampenborg, opposite Bellevue Strand.
question_meta: Skovfogedegen, a hollow oak at the edge of Jaegersborg Dyrehave 11 km north of Copenhagen, dates to about the year 1200: roughly 800 years old.
question_context: Skovfogedegen is not a Copenhagen tree in the ordinary sense. It stands 11 km north of the city, beside the road Strandvejen at the edge of Jaegersborg Dyrehave, the royal deer park at Klampenborg, opposite Bellevue Strand, and the S-train gets you within eight minutes' walk of it. Three dated Danish sources agree that it has been there since around the year 1200: the national encyclopedia, the historical-sites database Historisk Atlas, and a 2025 newspaper feature. The Danish Dendrological Society measured the trunk at 10.42 metres round, which is more than twice the girth of anything on this list inside the city, and recorded it hollow, 12.9 metres tall and living but weak. The heartwood rotted away long ago; an oak carries water and sugars in the growing layer just under the bark, so the shell holds. In the early 1800s a Catholic forest ranger used the cavity as a private prayer chamber, which is where the name comes from. Inside Copenhagen itself the oldest tree is the mulberry at Proviantgarden on Slotsholmen, tied to Christian IV's attempt at a Danish silk industry and likely 350 to 420 years old.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Copenhagen?
faq.a: Skovfogedegen, a hollow oak roughly 800 years old, dated by three Danish sources to around the year 1200. It stands 11 km north of the city at the edge of Jaegersborg Dyrehave. The oldest tree inside Copenhagen itself is the mulberry at Proviantgarden on Slotsholmen, likely 350 to 420 years old.

faq.q: Are all of these trees in Copenhagen?
faq.a: Thirteen of them are in or beside the city. Three are not: Skovfogedegen and Englaenderegen stand in and beside Jaegersborg Dyrehave at Klampenborg, and Klopstocks Eg is in Lyngby Aamose. All three are reachable by S-train in about 20 minutes, then 8 to 40 minutes on foot, so treat them as a half day out rather than part of a city walk.

faq.q: Which is the thickest tree on this list?
faq.a: Skovfogedegen, at 10.42 metres round and hollow through the middle. Inside the city the thickest is the pedunculate oak in Frederiksberg Have at 4.95 metres.

faq.q: Is the Palm House cycad really that old?
faq.a: Yes. Botanist Frederik Liebmann brought it from Mexico in 1842, and it remains the Botanical Garden's oldest living specimen, roughly 184 years old.

faq.q: Did Thorvaldsen really bring his own tree home from Italy?
faq.a: Tradition says so: the black locust beside Thorvaldsens Museum is said to have grown from seed the sculptor carried back when he returned to Copenhagen in 1838, though this is tradition rather than documented fact.

Along Husalle in Kongens Have, the king's garden beside Rosenborg Castle. Garden historians describe them as among the oldest living trees in Denmark, unlike the castle's two more formal linden avenues, which have been replanted repeatedly since the 1660s and 1700s.

trees.name: The Mulberry of Proviantgarden

location.address: Against the south-eastern gable of Proviantgarden, opposite the Royal Library, Slotsholmen, Copenhagen

trees.story:
King Christian IV tried to build a Danish silk industry the way his contemporaries elsewhere in Europe were doing it, by planting mulberry trees to feed silkworms, and Copenhagen has pointed at this tree as the survivor of that venture ever since. The Danish tree register records it as a black mulberry, Morus nigra, which is the fruiting mulberry rather than the white one silkworms are raised on, so read the silk connection as a story the city tells rather than a fact anybody has proved. Tradition credits a sailor who brought it home from Asia rather than a court gardener.

What the register does state is its age: one of the oldest mulberry trees in Denmark. It stands against the south-eastern gable of Proviantgarden, the naval arsenal Christian IV began in 1603 to supply his warships, facing the Royal Library, on ground that once fronted a working harbour basin where vessels docked to be provisioned and armed. It is five metres tall and grows the way old black mulberries do, leaning and sprawling rather than standing up straight. The silk venture itself mostly failed, Copenhagen's climate never suited silkworms the way Christian IV hoped, and the street name Silkegade nearby is the closest most Copenhageners now get to the story.
trees.access: Free, open access, public courtyard on Slotsholmen

trees.name: The Ancient Cycad of the Palm House

location.address: Palmehuset, Botanical Garden, Gothersgade 128, Copenhagen

trees.story: In 1842, the Danish botanist Frederik Liebmann sailed to Mexico and came home with, among other specimens, a small cycad that looked more like a stunted pineapple than anything resembling a tree. It has spent nearly two centuries since then growing at its own unhurried pace in Copenhagen's Botanical Garden, first at the garden's earlier city-centre site and then, from 1874, in the Palm House built specifically to keep tropical and subtropical plants alive through Danish winters. Cycads are not actually related to palms or ferns despite resembling both; they are among the oldest living groups of seed plants on Earth, largely unchanged since long before flowering plants existed, which makes a 184-year-old specimen barely middle-aged by the standards of its own family. Liebmann died in 1856 at just 43, only 14 years after bringing the plant home, but his cycad has outlived him by more than a century and a half and remains, by the garden's own account, its oldest living specimen and one of its genuine star attractions, a slow-growing plant that has simply outlasted everyone who ever went looking for one.
trees.access: Paid entry to Palmehuset (the outdoor Botanical Garden itself is free)
trees.transport: Norreport railway and metro station, short walk
trees.notes: The Liebmann collection date (1842), his death (1856), and the plant's status as the garden's oldest living specimen are given by the Danish Wikipedia entry on the Botanical Garden; only one detailed source found for this specific specimen, flagged accordingly, though the garden's own move to the current Palm House in 1874 is independently well documented. Coordinates are the garden's street address, not a surveyed position within the Palm House.
trees.how_to_recognise: Inside the Palm House, low and squat like a stunted pineapple rather than anything tree-shaped, and the garden's oldest living specimen.

trees.name: Thorvaldsen's Robinia

location.address: Beside Thorvaldsens Museum, Slotsholmen, Copenhagen

trees.story: Bertel Thorvaldsen spent more than 40 years in Rome becoming Europe's most celebrated Neoclassical sculptor before returning home to Copenhagen in 1838 to a hero's welcome, and this multi-stemmed black locust growing beside the museum built to house his life's work is said to have come home with him, grown from seed he carried back from Italy. Denmark's dendrological society surveyed the tree in 1995 and recorded a trunk over three metres around, splitting into several stems rather than one, and estimated its age at up to 155 years at that time, consistent with a planting soon after Thorvaldsen's actual return. That would put the tree, and not just the museum, among the direct physical legacies of a sculptor whose bronze and marble work now sits in collections from the Vatican to Warsaw. Black locust is not a species anyone would plant deliberately for its connection to fine art. It is a hardy, fast-growing tree valued more for binding loose soil and producing useful timber than for looking distinguished, which makes its adoption into Thorvaldsen's own story feel almost like an accident that stuck, a workmanlike species growing beside one of Europe's grandest personal museums, surveyed precisely enough by Danish tree recorders in 2008 to give this project one of its few confirmed coordinates.

trees.transport: Christianshavn metro station or Copenhagen Central Station, short walk across Slotsholmen
trees.notes: The only detailed source found is the Danish Dendrological Society's own tree register entry, which itself frames Thorvaldsen's personal planting as tradition ('possibly brought Robinia seeds') rather than documented fact; flagged accordingly. trees.name: The Husalle Lindens

location.address: Husalle, Kongens Have, Copenhagen

trees.story: Kongens Have is Copenhagen's oldest public park, laid out from 1606 for King Christian IV beside his new Rosenborg Castle, and its formal linden avenues were planted soon after: Kavalergangen and Damegangen, the two clipped alleys nearest the castle, date to around 1664 and 1700. Almost none of those original trees survive; both avenues have been replanted more than once in the four centuries since. Husalle, a third avenue running parallel to the garden's main axis a little further north, has fared differently: its lindens are described by garden historians as among the oldest living trees in Denmark, having escaped the repeated replacements that emptied the more formal avenues nearer the castle of their original planting. The garden itself has survived far more than ordinary wear. It has hosted royal pleasure grounds, public promenades, and, in recent years, a summer sound installation that lets speakers hidden in ten of its trees tell stories to anyone who walks close enough to trigger them, a very modern use for trees old enough to have shaded Danish kings centuries before recorded sound existed. Husalle's lindens do their storytelling the old way, simply by having outlasted almost everything planted around them.
trees.access: Free, open access, Kongens Have (public park, open daily)
trees.transport: Norreport railway and metro station, short walk
trees.notes: Kongens Have's founding (1606) and the c.1664/c.1700 planting of Kavalergangen and Damegangen are documented by the official Danish heritage agency's Trap Danmark entry and corroborated by Danish Wikipedia; both also state that virtually no original trees remain in those two avenues. The claim that Husalle's lindens are 'among the oldest in the country' comes from the same sources but without an exact planting date for that specific avenue, so the age range given here (300-360 years) reflects the garden's documented 1660s-1700s planting era generally rather than a dated record for Husalle itself. This entry represents the avenue as a whole rather than a single named tree.

trees.name: The Temple Tree of Landbohøjskolens Have

location.address: On the stone mound at the centre of Landbohojskolens Have (Fakultetets Fredede Have), Frederiksberg

trees.story:
This ginkgo is male, and the female it pollinates lives on the other side of the street. The two trees have never touched. The university library, writing up the garden's own history, calls it the largest ginkgo in the collection and gives 1883 as its planting year, which would make it about 143. That date comes from that one source and nowhere else, so read it as the garden's account rather than a measured fact.

It is planted in the middle of a large stone mound, which is a strange thing to do to a tree and suits this one. Ginkgo biloba is the last surviving member of a lineage older than flowering plants, and the Danish name for it, tempeltræet, points at the temple courtyards in China and Japan where the final populations were kept alive by monks while the wild ones disappeared. The garden around it was laid out in 1858 for the Royal Veterinary and Agricultural College and has been legally protected since 1965.

Protection is not immortality. The blood beech planted the year the garden opened, which the official heritage listing still describes as the thickest tree here, was felled in 2018. Nothing suggests the ginkgo has gone the same way and the species is famously hard to kill, but the newest dated confirmation we could find of this one is not recent. The garden is free and open from sunrise to sunset.

best_time.label: late October into November, when it turns gold and drops the whole crown within a week

trees.name: The Handkerchief Tree of Assistens

location.address: Assistens Kirkegård, Section A, near the northeast corner (Nørrebrogade / Kapelvej), Nørrebro, Copenhagen

trees.story:
What looks like flowers on this tree are leaves. For roughly two weeks in May the handkerchief tree hangs hundreds of paired white bracts through its crown, each pair a modified leaf wrapped around a small dark ball of actual flower, and Danish names it better than English does: duetræ, the dove tree. Davidia involucrata grows wild in the mountains of western China and reached Western cultivation only in 1904, through the plant hunter Ernest Wilson. It is still an uncommon thing to find in Denmark, and this one is multi-stemmed, so in May the bracts come at you from several directions at once.

Nobody wrote down when it was planted. The Danish Dendrological Society surveyed Assistens in November 2019, put a GPS point on this tree, measured 1.4 metres around its stems and recorded it alive and healthy. That is the honest limit of what is known here: a girth, not an age. The range on this page is inferred from that measurement and from how recently the species arrived in Danish gardens, not read off any record.

It stands in section A of a cemetery Copenhagen treats as a park. People run, read and eat their lunch here, a few hundred metres from the graves of Hans Christian Andersen and Søren Kierkegaard.

best_time.label: May, when the bracts open and the Danish name for it, dove tree, makes sense

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of Assistens

location.address: Assistens Kirkegård, Section B, just right of the entrance from Kapelvej, Nørrebro, Copenhagen

trees.story:
Every weeping beech is a graft, and on this one the join is in plain sight. About a metre up the trunk there is a visible union where a cutting of the pendulous form was fixed onto ordinary beech rootstock, and the surveyor who measured the tree in November 2019 noted that the grafted top is now putting on wood faster than the stock beneath it, so the trunk steps outward where the two meet. Look for that step before you look at the curtain.

The same survey recorded something less comfortable: a large wound at the base of the trunk. The tree was logged as alive, 3.29 metres round and 15 metres tall, but it is a healthy crown standing over an open injury, which is worth knowing rather than glossing over.

Weeping beech became a Danish cemetery fashion in the nineteenth century under the name sørgebøg, mourning beech, planted to hang over a grave the way a mourner leans over it. No planting date survives for this one. The 80 to 150 years on this page is worked back from the girth, not counted.

It stands in section B, just right of the Kapelvej entrance, which makes it the first serious tree most visitors to Assistens Kirkegård walk straight past.

trees.name: The Great Maple of Assistens

location.address: Assistens Kirkegård, Section C, roughly 10m southwest of the section's centre, Nørrebro, Copenhagen

trees.story:
The thickest tree at Assistens is also the least exotic species in it. At 4.19 metres round, this sycamore out-measures every tree the Danish Dendrological Society registered inside these walls, including the rarities people actually come to see, and it does it as a common European maple that seeds itself into any gap it can find. Twenty-two and a half metres tall, one trunk to about two metres up and then a fork into two, alive and healthy at the November 2019 survey, rated regionally noteworthy.

Assistens was not built for strolling. It opened in 1757 outside the city ramparts as an overflow burial ground, taking the dead that Copenhagen's crowded parish churchyards could no longer hold, and the famous names arrived later. The city then grew out past it, Nørrebro packed in around it, and the place slowly turned into what it is now: a walled park with graves in it, where on a warm afternoon the living comfortably outnumber the mourners.

No planting date exists for this maple, and the 100 to 180 years given here is inferred from its girth rather than counted. What is certain is the measurement, taken with GPS in the field, and that nothing else registered in this cemetery is thicker. Section C, a little southwest of the section's centre.

trees.name: The Beech by the Boat Trip

location.address: Frederiksberg Have, beside the Bådfarten (rowing-boat rental/canal boat trip), Frederiksberg

trees.story:
This beech is registered under the name of a boat trip. Danish dendrologists filed it as Bøgen ved Bådfarten, the beech by the boat trip, which makes it the easiest tree on this list to find: walk to the jetty in Frederiksberg Have where the flat-bottomed boats set off around the canals, and the tree is the big one standing over you. Its trunk is 4.68 metres round and 1.49 metres across, measured in October 2016 and recorded alive.

The water it stands beside is the reason the garden looks the way it does. Frederiksberg Have began around 1700 as a Baroque layout of straight lines below the royal palace, then was redrawn between 1798 and 1804 into a romantic landscape of winding canals, islands and staged views, which is the fashion this beech grew up inside. The garden is protected under Danish conservation law and free to walk into.

Its age is not documented anywhere. The 120 to 220 years here comes from girth alone, and the garden's own heritage listing is careful on the point: the trees it names as three centuries old are the lindens on Mathildehøj, not this beech. Only one other tree in Frederiksberg Have carries a thicker trunk, and it is a short walk away in the same garden.

best_time.label: late October, when the copper leaves come down onto the canal below it

trees.name: The Pedunculate Oak of Frederiksberg Have

location.address: Frederiksberg Have, Frederiksberg

trees.story:
This oak has no recorded birthday, but the garden gives it a ceiling. Frederiksberg Have was laid out as royal ground around 1700 and rebuilt between 1798 and 1804 into the romantic landscape park it still is, so whatever the tree's exact age, it cannot be older than the garden that had to exist before anyone planted in it. What was measured rather than guessed: 4.95 metres round, 28.8 metres tall, 1.58 metres through, surveyed by the Danish Dendrological Society in October 2016 and rated municipally noteworthy. That is the thickest trunk of any tree on this list standing inside the city itself; the oaks out in the deer park north of town are thicker again.

The 130 to 250 years on this page is arithmetic on that girth against how fast a parkland oak puts on wood, not a date from any record, and it should be read as the wide guess it is. A pedunculate oak growing in the open with room on every side thickens faster than one shut into a wood, which is exactly the situation here, and one reason the upper end of that range is probably generous.

The garden around it is public, protected and busy: lawns, canals, the palace up on its hill, boats in summer. The oak has watched the whole thing turn from a royal retreat into the city's back garden.

trees.name: The Honey Locust of Assistens

location.address: Assistens Kirkegård, Section E (near the middle of the section), Nørrebro, Copenhagen

trees.story:
Someone has been keeping notes on this tree since 1941. That year a Danish gardening magazine ran a feature on beautiful trees and included a honey locust in section E of Assistens cemetery. In 1949 Jens Østergaard came to measure it for a nationwide survey of Gleditsia triacanthos in Danish gardens, published in the Dendrological Society's 1952 yearbook: twelve metres tall, standing on what the surveyor recorded as former rampart ground, clay loam, listed as site number six of only thirty-five in the whole country. In November 2019 the Society came back with a GPS and a tape. Sixteen metres, 1.18 metres round, alive and healthy.

Four metres of growth in seventy years is exactly what this species should manage, which is what makes the paper trail worth more than a plaque. The same tree, in the same spot, written up three times across eighty years by people with no reason to exaggerate.

The thorns are what to look for, and you will have to look up. Honey locust usually arms its trunk with branched spikes at chest height. This one carries only a few, sitting two and a half to three metres up, out of reach and easy to walk straight past.

Assistens opened in 1760 as a burial ground for the poor, on ground outside the city ramparts, and Hans Christian Andersen lies a few minutes' walk from here. The honey locust was rare enough in Denmark to be worth cataloguing nationally. It still is.

trees.name: The Pacifier Tree

location.address: Frederiksberg Have, Frederiksberg

trees.story:
Every November this hornbeam gets harvested. Since 2004 parents in Frederiksberg have brought toddlers here to tie up the pacifier they have agreed to give up, and once a year the whole crop comes down so the tree can start again. Danish dendrologists list it on their national register under the name everyone else uses: Suttetræet, the pacifier tree.

That register entry is unusual for what it leaves out. Every other tree recorded in Frederiksberg Have carries a height, a girth, often a planting year. This one carries none of them. Nobody has measured it and nobody has dated it, so read any age attached to this tree as a guess rather than a measurement. It is a mature garden hornbeam. That is the whole of what is known.

Which is rather the point. Carpinus betulus is the workhorse of formal European gardens, planted by the thousand for its density and its patience under the shears, and Frederiksberg Have has been royal ground since about 1700 and a romantic landscape park since its rebuilding between 1798 and 1804. The garden's history is documented down to the decade. The tree's is not. What it has instead is twenty-two years of small plastic objects and a steady supply of three-year-olds making a decision.

Come in autumn if you want to see it fully loaded. The November harvest clears it back to bare branches.

trees.name: The Sky-Reacher of Assistens

location.address: Assistens Kirkegård, Section F (north field, near Nørrebrogade/the station area), Nørrebro, Copenhagen

trees.story:
Skyrækker, the Danish name for this species, means sky-reacher. At 15.5 metres this one does not out-top the big beeches and maples around it, but at 4.01 metres round it is the largest exotic tree the Danish Dendrological Society registered inside these cemetery walls, and the only Ailanthus they found here at all.

It also comes with an open question. The surveyors who measured it in November 2019 logged its condition as levende, svag: alive, but weak. They noted severe bark scraping low on the western side of the trunk, the kind of injury that interrupts the traffic between roots and crown. Nothing found since updates that note, so what stands behind this entry is one careful observation now about seven years old. If you go and find it changed, tell us.

No source gives its age either. Somewhere between sixty and a hundred and twenty years is an inference from girth alone, not a record.

Ailanthus altissima reached Europe from China in the eighteenth century as a fashionable exotic and is now better known for pushing up through railway ballast and cracked concrete anywhere it can get a root down. This one was planted on purpose, in a cemetery that collected rarities, and the handkerchief tree and the ginkgo a few paths away come from the same appetite. Assistens works as a public park as much as a burial ground, and that collection is a large part of why.

trees.name: Skovfogedegen

location.address: Strandvejen, opposite the northern end of Bellevue Strand, Klampenborg (edge of Jaegersborg Dyrehave)

trees.access: Free, no ticket. Stands on public ground beside the road Strandvejen at the edge of Jaegersborg Dyrehave (the royal deer park), opposite Bellevue Strand. Open at all times.
trees.transport: Klampenborg is roughly 10.9 km north of central Copenhagen. S-train line C (Kystbanen) from Copenhagen Central to Klampenborg station, about 16-20 minutes, then about 8 minutes on foot north along Strandvejen to the tree.

photo.license: CC BY-SA 3.0

trees.story:
Ten metres and 42 centimetres around, and empty in the middle. Skovfogedegen has lost its entire heartwood to rot, which an oak can survive: water and sugars travel in the thin growing layer just under the bark, so a hollow trunk is a shell that still works. Three dated Danish sources put the tree here since around the year 1200: the national encyclopedia, the historical-sites database Historisk Atlas, and a 2025 feature in the newspaper Kristeligt Dagblad. That makes it roughly 800 years old, and by a wide margin the oldest and thickest tree on this list. One untraced web page gives 500 years instead. Nothing stands behind it, and the three that agree are dated and named.

The hollow has been put to use. Johan Georg Weissler, a Catholic forest ranger who died in 1854, used the cavity as a private prayer chamber in the early 1800s, and skovfoged, forest ranger, is where the tree's name comes from. At other times the hole held peat.

The Danish Dendrological Society measured it at 12.9 metres tall and logged it living but weak in 2010. A photograph taken in March 2025 shows the same hollow trunk still standing. It is not a city tree: it grows beside the road Strandvejen at the edge of Jaegersborg Dyrehave, 11 km north of Copenhagen, opposite Bellevue Strand.

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are off and the hollow trunk and low crooked frame read clearly

trees.how_to_recognise: Ten metres and 42 centimetres round and completely hollow in the middle, standing beside the Strandvejen road opposite Bellevue beach.

trees.name: Klopstocks Eg

location.address: Prinsessestien, Lyngby Aamose (Molleaadalen), Kongens Lyngby

trees.access: Free, no ticket. Stands right beside Prinsessestien, a public path through Lyngby Aamose along Molleaadalen. Legally protected (fredet) since 1956, with a memorial plaque added in 1984, so a public authority has long treated it as open ground for visitors.
trees.transport: Kongens Lyngby is roughly 11.9 km northwest of central Copenhagen. S-train to Sorgenfri station (about 22-24 minutes from Copenhagen H), then about 15 minutes on foot west along Prinsessestien through Lyngby Aamose to the tree.

photo.license: CC BY-SA 4.0
photo.attribution: Finn Årup Nielsen, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.story:
Denmark protected this oak by law in 1956 and still cannot date it within four centuries. The Danish Dendrological Society's register gives 800 years as a maximum rather than an estimate, which is a different kind of number: the most the tree could be, not the best guess at what it is. So the range here runs from 400 to 800 years, and nobody has narrowed it.

What has been measured: 6.05 metres round, 1.93 metres through, alive at the last field report. A storm in 2013 broke off a large branch and the tree carried on without further loss.

The name belongs to Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock, the German poet who came to Denmark in 1751 at the invitation of Frederik V, stayed twenty years, and spent his summers at Gramlille on Lyngby Hovedgade, a short walk from here. Nothing is recorded about what he did under this particular tree. It carries his name the way a street does, by association with the neighbourhood he lived in. It has also been called Monrads Eg, after D.G. Monrad. A memorial plaque went up in 1984.

The oak stands right beside Prinsessestien, a public path through Lyngby Aamose in the Molleaadalen valley, about 12 km northwest of Copenhagen and a quarter of an hour on foot from Sorgenfri station.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.how_to_recognise: Right beside the Prinsessestien path through the meadow, 6.05 metres round, with a memorial plaque put up in 1984.

trees.name: Englaenderegen

location.address: Jaegersborg Dyrehave, by Magasindammen, northeast of Eremitageslottet

trees.access: Free, no ticket, and marked wheelchair-accessible on the Nature Agency's own listing. Stands in the open deer park of Jaegersborg Dyrehave, a public UNESCO-listed royal hunting landscape with no gates or opening hours beyond dusk closing for cars.
trees.transport: Central Copenhagen to Dyrehaven's edge is roughly 12.6 km. S-train line C to Klampenborg station (about 16-20 minutes from Copenhagen Central), then a walk of roughly 35-40 minutes through the deer park, past Eremitageslottet, to reach Magasindammen; this tree sits deeper into the park than the entrance, so the walk-in is the honest, longer part of the trip.

photo.license: CC BY-SA 2.0

trees.story:
This oak was dying, and treasure hunters saved it by accident. Generations of digging around its roots broke up the packed soil and let air back in, which is what the Danish Dendrological Society's register credits with its recovery. Nobody was trying to help the tree. They were looking for a chest of money.

The name, Englaenderegen, the Englishman's oak, comes from the British siege of Copenhagen in 1807. Two soldiers, tired of service, are said to have stolen their regiment's pay chest and buried it beside a freestanding oak northeast of the Hermitage. Neither came back for it, and one confessed on his deathbed to a priest. Searches followed for over a hundred years, including one made at the request of Queen Victoria, and nothing has ever been found. The chest is legend. The holes were real, and they are the part that mattered.

The register measures the trunk at 5.46 metres round and 1.74 metres through, and dates it at 240 to 360 years using a growth formula applied to 1995 measurements, which puts it at roughly 270 to 390 now. It stands by the pond Magasindammen in Jaegersborg Dyrehave, the royal deer park north of Copenhagen, and the Nature Agency marks the site wheelchair accessible. Getting there is the long part: 35 to 40 minutes on foot from Klampenborg station, past Eremitageslottet.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.how_to_recognise: A freestanding oak by the Magasindammen pond northeast of the Hermitage, 5.46 metres round, in open deer park rather than in woodland.

trees.name: The Hawthorn of Nordpolen

location.address: Nordpolen, the wild green corner of De Gamles By, north of Norre Alle, facing Tagensvej, Norrebro

verified_sources: Dansk Traeregister (Danish Tree Register), id 1108, position verified 10-09-2018: https://www.dendron.dk/dtr/detaljer.asp?Individual_id=1108

Red Byens Traeer (a citizen blog documenting Norrebro's green spaces, independent of the register's own citation), which names this specific old crooked hawthorn at Nordpolen and describes it as older than Norrebro itself: http://redbyenstraeer.blogspot.com/2019/01/nordpolen-og-de-gamles-by-del-1.html and http://redbyenstraeer.blogspot.com/2019/02/nordpolen-og-de-gamles-by-del-2.html
trees.access: Free, open green area; a public path crosses Nordpolen near De Gamles By, and the hawthorn stands beside it.
trees.transport: Norrebro station (S-train) or bus 6A/350S along Tagensvej, then roughly 15-20 minutes on foot to De Gamles By.
trees.verify_notes: One of the last remnants of an old common/heath (overdrev) that predates the surrounding Norrebro neighbourhood, per both the register and the Red Byens Traeer blog, which independently calls it 'the magical white hawthorn, older than Norrebro itself' and documents a local campaign that kept a planned school/diabetes-centre building project off Nordpolen specifically to protect the green corner and this tree (building plans were paused as of August 2018 per the register's own legend). Species is unresolved to exact Crataegus species in the register (Crataegus sp.), so the page should ask the reader. Growth form: gnarled/twisted (forvredet-forkroblet), which matches an old hedgerow-relict hawthorn rather than a planted specimen. Register position verified 10-09-2018.
trees.story:
A school and a diabetes centre were planned for this corner of Nørrebro, and the plans were paused to keep the green ground, and this hawthorn on it, intact. The register's own note records the pause as of August 2018.

What the campaigners were defending is a remnant. Nordpolen is one of the last surviving pieces of the old common, the overdrev, that lay here before Nørrebro was built across it, so the hawthorn belongs to the ground rather than to anybody's planting plan. Red Byens Træer, a local blog that has gone through this quarter tree by tree, calls it the magical white hawthorn, older than Nørrebro itself. The register puts it at 2.21 metres round and 8.5 metres tall and describes its form as twisted and stunted, which is what a hedgerow survivor looks like standing next to a planted specimen.

It is a small tree by the standards of this list and it has outlasted everything around it, which is the whole point of it. The hospital campus of De Gamles By sits on one side and Tagensvej runs on the other.

Nobody has dated it, and nobody has settled which hawthorn it is: the register files it as Crataegus sp. and leaves the species open. If you know which one it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, twisted and stunted rather than straight, 2.21 metres round under a crown only 8.5 metres tall. It stands in the rough green corner of Nordpolen, beside the path that crosses it.

trees.name: Trepileegen, the Three-Willow Oak of Dyrehaven

location.address: Jaegersborg Dyrehave (the royal deer park), Lyngby-Taarbaek Kommune, near the park's cluster of named veteran oaks

verified_sources: Linda's netsted, an independent Danish hiking blog describing a walk past Dyrehaven's named giant oaks, which identifies Trepileegen by name and describes it as enormous, with a natural step-like base that makes it climbable: https://lindasnetsted.wordpress.com/2017/05/06/koebenhavn-egetraeer-i-dyrehaven/
trees.access: Free, open daily; Jaegersborg Dyrehave is a public royal deer park (free-roaming red, sika and fallow deer share the park, keep a respectful distance).
trees.transport: Klampenborg station (S-train, line C), then roughly a 30-40 minute walk into the deer park; the park is large (about 11 square kilometres) and has no closer station.
trees.verify_notes: IMPORTANT correction: the register's headline girth of 9.65 m is measured at a different trunk height than its own legend, which states the circumference was 8.90 m at 1.30 m above ground in March 2017. Use 890 cm, not 965, as the comparable trunk figure. Two-stemmed/multi-stemmed growth form per the register. Age is DERIVED, not sourced: girth 890 cm gives a diameter of about 283 cm; applying the standard open-grown oak ageing multiplier (roughly 1.25 to 2.0 years per cm of diameter, the low end for a pasture-grown oak with unrestricted growth, the high end for a more constrained one) gives a band of roughly 350 to 570 years, rounded here to 350-550. This is a calculation, not a measured age; state the basis on the page. Name meaning: 'Trepileegen' is not confidently explained by any source found; render the gloss as given in the brief ('Three-Willow Oak') but do not assert a false etymology in the story.
trees.story:
Measured at chest height in March 2017, this oak came to 8.90 metres round. The register's headline figure of 9.65 metres is taken at a different height on the same trunk, which is how one tree ends up carrying two sizes. The lower number is the one to use when comparing it with anything else.

Either way it is one of the giants of Jægersborg Dyrehave, the royal deer park north of the city, where red, sika and fallow deer still have the run of eleven square kilometres. The oak grows on more than one stem and its base steps outward near the ground; a Danish hiking blog that walked the park's named oaks describes that base as making the tree climbable, which is the sort of detail only somebody who put their hands on it would write down.

Nobody has cored it, so the age is arithmetic rather than a record. A girth of 8.90 metres gives a trunk about 2.8 metres across, and standard growth rates for an oak grown in the open put that somewhere between roughly 350 and 550 years. The band is wide because the method is.

The name Trepileegen translates as the Three-Willow Oak. What the three willows were, or whether they ever stood here, is not explained by any source we found.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 8.90 metres round at chest height on more than one stem, stepping outward at the base. It is the widest of the named oaks in this part of Dyrehaven, about 100 metres from Kuppelegen.

trees.name: The Field Maple of Hans Tavsens Park

location.address: Hans Tavsens Park, opposite Jesper Brochmands Gade, Norrebro

trees.access: Free, open public park (Hans Tavsens Park), adjacent to Assistens Cemetery.
trees.transport: Norrebro station (S-train), about 15 minutes on foot.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: only the register carries this tree; no independent second source found describing this specific specimen (general pages about Hans Tavsens Park exist but do not mention it). The register's own claim is strong and worth using with attribution: it is currently Denmark's third-thickest field maple, though two field maples in Dragsholm Park are noted as two registrations of the same tree, which affects the ranking's arithmetic. Several larger branches have been sawn off the crown and some smaller branches are dry, per the register's legend, so the tree shows some decline; nothing suggests it is not alive.
trees.story:
The Danish Tree Register calls this the third thickest field maple currently standing in Denmark. That is the register's claim and nobody else repeats it, and the register complicates its own arithmetic in the same breath: two of the maples in the ranking, both in Dragsholm Park, look like two entries for one tree.

Rank aside, the tree is odd for its species. Acer campestre is a small thing, more often clipped into a hedge than allowed to become anything, and this one has 4.03 metres of trunk and 12 metres of height in a public park in Nørrebro, opposite Jesper Brochmands Gade and a few minutes from Assistens Cemetery.

It has had work done. Several of the larger branches have been sawn out of the crown and some of the smaller ones are dry, recorded by the surveyor who checked the position in April 2019. That reads as a tree being managed rather than a tree failing, and nothing in the record suggests otherwise.

No second source carries this maple at all, so everything above rests on one register entry. Nobody has dated it either, and we have not tried to work an age out of the girth. If you know when this part of Hans Tavsens Park was planted, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the small five-lobed leaves of a field maple on a trunk 4.03 metres round, with sawn stubs where large branches have been taken out. It stands in Hans Tavsens Park opposite Jesper Brochmands Gade.

trees.name: Kuppelegen, the Dome Oak of Dyrehaven

location.address: Jaegersborg Dyrehave (the royal deer park), Lyngby-Taarbaek Kommune, about 100 metres from Trepileegen

verified_sources: Linda's netsted hiking blog, which names Kuppelegen among Dyrehaven's giant oaks, though the author notes uncertainty telling it apart from a neighbouring oak (Stokkerupegen) in the same cluster: https://lindasnetsted.wordpress.com/2017/05/06/koebenhavn-egetraeer-i-dyrehaven/
trees.access: Free, open daily; Jaegersborg Dyrehave is a public royal deer park.
trees.transport: Klampenborg station (S-train, line C), then roughly a 30-40 minute walk into the deer park.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED for identification: the independent hiking blog found as a second source names Kuppelegen but its author admits uncertainty distinguishing it from a similar neighbouring oak in the same cluster (Stokkerupegen), so treat the second source as supportive rather than fully independent confirmation. The register's own position (verified 2008) is the reliable part. 'Kuppel' means dome/cupola, describing the crown shape. Age DERIVED from girth 863 cm (diameter about 275 cm) using the open-grown oak multiplier of roughly 1.25-2.0 years/cm, giving approximately 340-550 years, rounded to 350-550.
trees.story:
The hiker who went out to find this oak came back unsure of the find. That account of Dyrehaven's named giants lists Kuppelegen and admits it could not be confidently separated from Stokkerupegen, a similar oak standing in the same group. So take the position from the register, which checked it in 2008, and take the walking account as support rather than proof.

Kuppel means dome, and the name describes the crown: wide and low rather than reaching. At 17.2 metres this is the shortest of the park's big named oaks and among the widest, 8.63 metres round, standing about a hundred metres from Trepileegen.

The age is a calculation, not a record. A trunk 8.63 metres in circumference is roughly 2.75 metres across, and growth rates for oaks grown in the open put that between about 350 and 550 years. Call it old and leave the century open.

Go slowly at the end of the walk. These oaks stand in a cluster and more than one of them is enormous, which is exactly how the hiker came unstuck. The park is free and open every day, and it is a long way in: from Klampenborg station the walk is 30 to 40 minutes, with free-roaming red, sika and fallow deer for company most of it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, domed and spread wide rather than tall, only 17.2 metres high over a trunk 8.63 metres round. It stands about 100 metres from Trepileegen, which is taller and grows on several stems.

trees.name: Vorteegen, the Wart Oak of Dyrehaven

location.address: Jaegersborg Dyrehave (the royal deer park), Lyngby-Taarbaek Kommune, on the open prairie-like grassland area

verified_sources: Linda's netsted hiking blog, which names Vorteegen on the park's open grassland and notes it did not visibly show the wart-like growths its name suggests: https://lindasnetsted.wordpress.com/2017/05/06/koebenhavn-egetraeer-i-dyrehaven/
trees.access: Free, open daily; Jaegersborg Dyrehave is a public royal deer park.
trees.transport: Klampenborg station (S-train, line C), then roughly a 30-40 minute walk into the deer park.
trees.verify_notes: IMPORTANT correction: use the register's legend figures, not its headline ones. In March 2017 the girth was measured at 8.48 m and the height at 16.5 m; the headline figures (8.41 m girth, 16.8 m height) are the earlier measurement. 'Vorteegen' means 'the Wart Oak', referring to wart-like burrs on the bark; single-stemmed. Age DERIVED from girth 848 cm (diameter about 270 cm) using the open-grown oak multiplier of roughly 1.25-2.0 years/cm, giving approximately 335-540 years, rounded to 325-550.
trees.story:
This oak is called the Wart Oak, for the wart-like burrs on its bark, and the hiker who walked out to look at them recorded that the tree did not visibly show any.

It is worth the walk regardless. Vorteegen stands on a single stem out on the open grassland in Jægersborg Dyrehave, 8.48 metres round and 16.5 metres tall by the register's own legend, measured in March 2017. The headline figures on the same entry, 8.41 metres and 16.8 metres, are the earlier survey: between the two the girth gained seven centimetres and the recorded height lost thirty, which is the ordinary wobble of measuring a living tree from the ground.

Nobody has cored it and no planting record exists, so the age is derived. A circumference of 8.48 metres is a trunk roughly 2.7 metres across, and standard growth rates for an oak grown in the open put that between about 325 and 550 years.

The open ground is why it looks like this. A tree with nothing crowding it spends its growth sideways, so the trunk is enormous and the crown is only as high as it needs to be. The deer graze around it, free-roaming red, sika and fallow, and the park is free and open every day.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the single trunk, 8.48 metres round, standing alone out on the open grassland rather than among other oaks. It is 16.5 metres tall, shorter than its girth suggests, with no close neighbours.

trees.name: The Hornbeam of Grondalsparken

location.address: Grondalsparken, about 100 metres southwest of Grondal station, east of the path

trees.access: Free, open public park (Grondalsparken), which runs as a green corridor along the railway between Damhussoen and Borups Alle.
trees.transport: Grondal station (S-train), about 100 metres, a couple of minutes on foot.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: register-only, no independent second source found for this individual tree; general histories of Grondalsparken (laid out 1930-1939 by city gardener Fabricius-Hansen) exist but do not name it. IMPORTANT caveat on the measurement: the register's own legend says the tree has 4 to 5 stems ('4-5 stammer'), so 416 cm is a multi-stem measurement, NOT a single trunk girth. Do not present it as a thickest-trunk figure; describe it as a wide multi-stemmed hornbeam instead. Alive and healthy per the register (Levende, sund).
trees.story:
The figure in the register, 4.16 metres, is not a trunk. The surveyor counted four or five stems and put the tape around the lot of them, so this is a wide multi-stemmed hornbeam rather than a thick-trunked one, which is worth saying plainly because the number flatters it otherwise.

What it is instead is a big healthy hornbeam 16.5 metres tall, a hundred metres from Grøndal station, in a green corridor that follows the railway between Damhussøen and Borups Allé. Grøndalsparken was laid out between 1930 and 1939 to the design of the city gardener Fabricius-Hansen. Nothing in the record dates this tree to that work, so it is not dated here either.

Several stems out of one base is the ordinary shape for Carpinus betulus. It is the classic coppice and hedging tree of northern Europe, cut for centuries for tool handles and firewood because the wood is harder than oak, and it answers cutting by coming back as a cluster rather than a trunk.

Only the register carries this tree. It was recorded alive and healthy when the position was checked in November 2019, and no other source names it at all. If you know anything about its history, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the four or five stems rising together from one base, 4.16 metres round the whole group, under a crown 16.5 metres tall. It stands east of the path, about 100 metres southwest of Grøndal station.

trees.name: Raunkiaer's Oak, the Burnt Oak of Dyrehaven

location.address: Jaegersborg Dyrehave (the royal deer park), Lyngby-Taarbaek Kommune, on the oak between Dalvej and Chausseen

verified_sources: N.E. Holten, 'Kaempeege i Danmark: En beskrivelse af de 30 tykkeste traeer', Dansk Dendrologisk Aarsskrift, bind 16, 1998, pages 25-111 (a published survey of Denmark's 30 thickest oaks, cited by the register as the origin of this tree's 1998 measurements; a genuinely separate authored source from the register's own personal-observation citations).
trees.access: Free, open daily; Jaegersborg Dyrehave is a public royal deer park.
trees.transport: Klampenborg station (S-train, line C), then roughly a 30-40 minute walk into the deer park.
trees.verify_notes: Carries two alternative names in the register besides its formal one: 'Den Braendte Eg' (The Burnt Oak) and 'Raunkiaers Eg' (Raunkiaer's Oak, after the Danish botanist Christen C. Raunkiaer, known for his work on plant life-forms, who studied Dyrehaven's ancient oaks). Measurements (820 cm girth, 21 m height) are explicitly from 1998 per the register's own comment, so the tree is likely a little larger today; state the measurement date. Single-stemmed. Age DERIVED from the 1998 girth (diameter about 261 cm) using the open-grown oak multiplier of roughly 1.25-2.0 years/cm, giving approximately 325-525 years as of that measurement.
trees.story:
This oak carries three names and the most interesting one is unexplained. Beside its formal entry the register lists Den Brændte Eg, the Burnt Oak, and Raunkiærs Eg, after Christen C. Raunkiær, the Danish botanist who classified plants by life-form and who studied Dyrehaven's ancient oaks. What burned, and when, no source we found says.

The measurements are dated and unusually solid: 8.20 metres round and 21 metres tall, recorded in 1998 and published in N.E. Holten's survey of the thirty thickest oaks in Denmark in the Danish Dendrological Yearbook. Most trees on this list rest on a register field. This one rests on a printed survey, and it has had nearly thirty growing seasons since, so the trunk is wider now than the number says.

The age is derived rather than recorded, as everywhere in this park. A girth of 8.20 metres gives a trunk about 2.6 metres across, which standard growth rates for an open-grown oak put between roughly 325 and 525 years as of that 1998 measurement.

It grows on one stem between Dalvej and Chausseen, taller than most of the park's fat old oaks and not much thinner. The deer go where they like and the park is free, open daily.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the single trunk, 8.20 metres round when it was measured in 1998, under a crown 21 metres tall, taller than the other named oaks of this size. It stands between Dalvej and Chausseen.

trees.name: The Weeping Silver Lime of J.C. Jacobsens Have

location.address: J.C. Jacobsens Have, Carlsberg Byen, at the southern end by the path around the southwest lawn

verified_sources: Carlsberg Byen's own account of J.C. Jacobsens Have, which confirms the garden (laid out 1848 by landscape architect Rudolph Rothe as J.C. Jacobsen's private garden, opened to the public in 2009, now a protected monument) as the historic planting ground for trees the brewer brought home from his travels: https://www.carlsbergbyen.dk/om-carlsberg-byen/byrum-i-carlsberg-byen/jc-jacobsens-have
trees.access: Free, open public park (J.C. Jacobsens Have), part of Carlsberg Byen.
trees.transport: Carlsberg station (S-train), about 10 minutes on foot.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: the Carlsberg Byen source confirms the garden's history and its collection of travel-brought trees in general, but does not independently name this specific weeping silver lime, so treat the second source as strong context rather than a dedicated confirmation. Several main branches are held together with wires per the register's legend, suggesting some structural weakness/decline being managed. Danish common name given in the register is 'Ungarsk Solvlind' (Hungarian Silver Lime), a colloquial name for this weeping form of Tilia tomentosa; the register itself flags the translation as unauthorised.
trees.story:
The main branches of this lime are held together with wire. The register noted the cables when it checked the tree in April 2019, which means somebody is managing a weakness in the crown rather than waiting to see, and it has not stopped the tree becoming one of the largest things in the garden: 4.77 metres round and 27.5 metres tall.

The garden is J.C. Jacobsens Have, laid out in 1848 by the landscape architect Rudolph Rothe as the private grounds of the brewer who founded Carlsberg, and planted over the years with trees he brought home from his travels. It opened to the public in 2009 and is a protected monument now. Whether this particular lime was one of his own imports is not recorded in anything we found: the Carlsberg account describes the garden and not its individual trees, so the tree itself rests on the register entry.

Tilia tomentosa 'Petiolaris' is the weeping form of the silver lime. The leaves are dark on top and white-felted underneath, hung on long stalks, so the whole crown turns pale and flickers whenever there is wind. The Danish register files it under Ungarsk Sølvlind, Hungarian silver lime, a local name for the same tree.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, hanging and pale, flashing white undersides of leaves in any wind, with steel cables bracing the main branches. It stands at the southern end by the path around the southwest lawn.

trees.name: The Field Maple of Kaerholmen

location.address: Grondalsparken, facing the building at Kaerholmen

trees.access: Free, open public park (Grondalsparken).
trees.transport: Grondal station (S-train), about 10 minutes on foot along the park.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: register-only, no independent second source found. A different individual from cop_022's hornbeam and from cop_019's field maple; the register numbers it 'Navr 2' to distinguish it from the Hans Tavsens Park specimen. Solitary tree, multi-stemmed or multi-branched from about 1 metre height per the register's legend. Alive and healthy (Levende, sund).
trees.story:
Copenhagen has two field maples worth crossing town for, and the register tells them apart by numbering: this one is filed as Navr 2. It is the taller of the pair and the slimmer, 3.60 metres round and 15.5 metres high, against 4.03 metres and 12 metres for the maple in Hans Tavsens Park.

It stands on its own in Grøndalsparken, facing the building at Kærholmen, and it branches from about a metre up, so what you get above head height is several heavy limbs rather than one continuing trunk. A solitary field maple is the interesting part. Acer campestre spends most of its life in Denmark as hedge material, cut back every few years and never allowed to become anything; this one was left alone long enough to turn into a tree, in a park that runs as a green strip along the railway.

The register recorded it as alive and healthy when the position was checked in November 2019, and the register is the only source that carries it. Nobody else has written it up, nobody has dated it, and no age is offered here because none can be honestly derived.

If you know when this stretch of the park was planted, tell us and we will put it in.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the small five-lobed maple leaves on a solitary tree that splits into heavy limbs about a metre up. It faces the building at Kærholmen, standing alone rather than in the park's plantings.

trees.name: The Fern-leaved Beech of the National Gallery

location.address: Statens Museum for Kunst (the National Gallery of Denmark), by the northeastern gable of the museum, facing Oster Anlaeg

verified_sources: Dansk Arkitektur Center on the museum's garden (Museumshaven), confirming it was reopened in 2014 as a space fully open toward Oster Voldgade and Solvgade, inviting passers-by in directly, and functions as public space around the clock: https://dac.dk/magazine/steder/museumshaven-ved-statens-museum-for-kunst-337
trees.access: Free, the museum's own grounds are open to the public around the clock as part of Oster Anlaeg; no ticket needed to reach the tree (a ticket is only needed to enter the museum building itself).
trees.transport: Osterport station (S-train and regional trains), about 10 minutes on foot through Oster Anlaeg.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: the DAC source confirms the museum garden's open, public character but does not name this specific tree, so treat as access confirmation rather than a dedicated second source for the tree itself. Many root-sprung branches, several oddly sawn from the trunk for reasons the register's own recorder could not explain, per its legend. 'Bregnebog' (fern-leaved beech) has deeply cut, fern-like leaves, a distinct beech cultivar.
trees.story:
Somebody has sawn branches off this beech and the surveyor who recorded it could not work out why. The register's note describes several oddly cut stubs on the trunk, along with a mass of branches sprouting from low down, and offers no explanation for either. Whoever did the cutting left no reason behind.

The tree is a fern-leaved beech, 4.37 metres round and 18 metres tall, standing at the northeastern gable of Statens Museum for Kunst with Øster Anlæg opening out behind it. 'Laciniata' is a form of the ordinary European beech whose leaves are cut into narrow, deeply toothed lobes, so at a glance the crown does not read as beech at all. In late October it does what every beech does and turns copper, on leaves shaped like fern fronds.

The museum garden was reopened in 2014 deliberately unfenced toward Øster Voldgade and Sølvgade, so the ground the tree stands on is public around the clock. The ticket is only for the building.

Only the register carries the tree itself. The museum and its garden are well documented; this beech is not, beyond one survey in December 2019 that measured it and wrote down the cut branches nobody could account for.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, cut into narrow lobes like fern fronds rather than the smooth oval of an ordinary beech. It stands at the northeastern gable of the museum, facing Øster Anlæg.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of J.C. Jacobsens Have

location.address: J.C. Jacobsens Have, Carlsberg Byen, on the round lawn to the west, about 20 metres from the honorary residence

verified_sources: Carlsberg Byen's own account of J.C. Jacobsens Have and its history as brewer J.C. Jacobsen's private collection of trees brought home from his travels: https://www.carlsbergbyen.dk/om-carlsberg-byen/byrum-i-carlsberg-byen/jc-jacobsens-have
trees.access: Free, open public park (J.C. Jacobsens Have), part of Carlsberg Byen.
trees.transport: Carlsberg station (S-train), about 10 minutes on foot.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: as with the garden's other Carlsberg trees, the Carlsberg Byen source confirms the garden's general history but not this specific plane by name; treat as context. Very uneven bark low on the trunk per the register's legend. Single-stemmed, healthy (Levende, sund).
trees.story:
This is an eastern Mediterranean tree standing 5.80 metres round in a Copenhagen brewery garden. Platanus orientalis grows wild from the Balkans east into Iran, and this one is 22 metres tall on a single stem on the round lawn west of the honorary residence, a long way north of anywhere it would seed itself.

The garden explains the geography. J.C. Jacobsens Have was laid out in 1848 as the private grounds of the brewer who founded Carlsberg, and it was stocked over decades with trees he brought back from his travels. It opened to the public in 2009 and is a protected monument. Whether this plane was one of his own imports is not written down anywhere we could find, so the tree itself rests on the register entry that measured it in 2019 and recorded it healthy.

Low on the trunk the bark has gone lumpy and uneven, which the surveyor noted specifically. Higher up it does what planes do, shedding in plates to leave the trunk mottled cream and olive.

The leaves are the giveaway if you are comparing it with Copenhagen's London planes: the oriental plane is cut far more deeply, into narrow pointed lobes that run most of the way to the leaf stalk.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, cut into narrow lobes almost to the stalk, deeper than any London plane, and by the lumpy bark low on the trunk. It stands on the round lawn about 20 metres from the honorary residence.

trees.name: The Beech of Holmens Kirkegard

location.address: Holmens Kirkegard, by the western path, about 50 metres from the northern corner

verified_sources: Hovedstadshistorie.dk's history of Holmens Kirkegard, confirming it as Copenhagen's oldest cemetery still in use (consecrated 1666, the navy's own burial ground, also called Skovkirkegard/Badsmandskirkegard) and open to visitors: https://www.hovedstadshistorie.dk/oestervold-2/holmens-kirkegaard/

Large root buttresses, described in the register's legend as 'almost an elephant's foot half a metre up the trunk'. Single-stemmed, healthy.
trees.story:
The surveyor who measured this beech wrote that the base is almost an elephant's foot, half a metre up the trunk. That is the register's own phrase, and it is a fair description of what root buttresses do to an old beech: the trunk stops being round and starts spreading into the ground in folds.

Above the folds it is a straightforward giant, one stem, 5.40 metres round and 19.5 metres tall, recorded healthy at the December 2018 survey. It stands by the western path of Holmens Kirkegård, about fifty metres from the northern corner.

The ground is the oldest working cemetery in Copenhagen. Holmens Kirkegård was consecrated in 1666 as the burial ground of the navy, which is why it is also called Skovkirkegården and Bådsmandskirkegården, and it is still in use. Nobody has dated the beech, so it is not being credited with the whole of that. What can be said is that it grew up in a burial ground rather than a park, which is a quieter kind of ground and usually an older one.

Only the register names the tree itself. The cemetery's history is well documented and says nothing about this beech in particular.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the base, spread into folds like an elephant's foot about half a metre up, under a single trunk 5.40 metres round. It stands by the western path, roughly 50 metres from the cemetery's northern corner.

trees.name: The Japanese Pagoda Tree of Rolighedsvej

location.address: Immediately east of Sankt Thomas Kirke, at the junction of Rolighedsvej and L.I. Brandes Alle, Frederiksberg

trees.access: Free, stands on public ground at a street corner beside Sankt Thomas Kirke.
trees.transport: Fasanvej station (Copenhagen Metro, M1/M2), about 10 minutes on foot.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: register-only, no independent second source found. Was heavily pruned a few years before the 2022 survey and carries large bark wounds on its south and east sides over the lowest 2 metres, per the register's legend, so it has visible past damage though it is recorded as alive.
trees.story:
The Japanese pagoda tree is not Japanese. Styphnolobium japonicum comes from China and was named from cultivated trees in Japan, where Europeans first saw it, which is the sort of accident that sticks for three centuries.

This one stands on a street corner in Frederiksberg, immediately east of Sankt Thomas Kirke where Rolighedsvej meets L.I. Brandes Allé, 3.15 metres round and 12 metres tall. It has had a hard time of it. A few years before the 2022 survey somebody cut it back heavily, and it carries large bark wounds on its south and east sides over the lowest two metres of trunk. The register recorded it alive.

It is worth knowing what the species does in late summer, because almost nothing else does it. The pagoda tree flowers in August and September, cream-coloured and in loose sprays, at the point in the year when every other flowering tree in the city has long finished. Whether this pruned and wounded specimen still puts on a full show is not something any source records.

No source but the register carries this tree at all. If you pass it and can say how the crown is doing, that would be worth more to us than another measurement.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the wounds, large patches of missing bark on the south and east sides of the lowest two metres, and by the hard-pruned crown. It stands on the corner immediately east of Sankt Thomas Kirke.

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of Allegade

location.address: A park by Allegade 17, Frederiksberg (Allegade runs along the east side of Frederiksberg Have and holds a public rose garden entered from Allegade 20; our sources describe the tree as standing in 'the park at Allegade' but do not name the exact plot)

trees.access: Likely free and open (Allegade holds a public rose garden, Rosenhaven, entered from number 20), but our sources do not confirm this exact tree sits on that public plot rather than an adjoining private one; treat as needing a reader's confirmation before treating access as fully settled.
trees.transport: Frederiksberg station (Metro M1/M2 and S-train) or Fasanvej station, about 10 minutes on foot.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED, access uncertain: a Frederiksberg municipality news item was found by search describing 'one of the municipality's oldest trees, a winged walnut about 200 years old' at Allegade, which would match this tree closely, but the page returned a 404 when fetched directly and the figure could not be confirmed on the source itself, so it is NOT used as a sourced age here per the search-summary caution rule. Do not add an age to this tree until the claim is confirmed on an actual page. Register-only for existence/species/position. Single-stemmed.
trees.story:
Everything about this tree is settled except whether you can walk up to it. The register has it at 3.90 metres round and 20 metres tall on a single stem, position checked in September 2016, described as standing in the park at Allégade 17 in Frederiksberg. What no source we found will confirm is which plot that is. Allégade has a public rose garden, Rosenhaven, entered from number 20, and it also has private ground behind it, and our sources do not say which side of that line this wingnut is on. Go expecting to look rather than to stand underneath, and tell us what you find.

It is worth the uncertainty. Pterocarya fraxinifolia is the Caucasian wingnut, a tree of the wet forests between the Black Sea and northern Iran, with long pinnate leaves like an ash and chains of small winged nuts that hang down through the summer. It suckers hard, so old ones are often surrounded by their own offspring.

No age is offered here. Nothing we could verify dates it, and nothing in the record supports deriving one, so the field stays empty rather than being filled with a guess. If you know when it went in, tell us. Only the register carries the tree.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the long ash-like leaves, many leaflets to a stalk, and the hanging chains of winged nuts in summer. It is a single trunk 3.90 metres round in the park ground by Allégade 17.

trees.name: The London Plane of Landbohojskolens Have

location.address: Landbohojskolens Have (the Royal Veterinary and Agricultural University's garden, now University of Copenhagen Frederiksberg Campus), behind the former auditorium VII (now the festival auditorium)

verified_sources: University of Copenhagen's own history of the garden's old trees, confirming it was inaugurated in 1858 and holds trees that have stood for over 150 years, including large multi-stemmed specimens: https://kub.ku.dk/biblioteker/frederiksberg/landbohoejskolens-historie/life150/haven/de_gamle_trer/
trees.access: Free, open public garden (Landbohojskolens Have), part of the University of Copenhagen's Frederiksberg Campus.
trees.transport: Fasanvej station (Copenhagen Metro, M1/M2), about 10 minutes on foot.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: the university's own garden-history page confirms the garden and its old trees in general (naming zelkovas, a golden weeping ash, ash and chestnut collections) but does not specifically name this plane tree, so treat as strong context rather than a dedicated second source. Single-stemmed, healthy (Levende, sund).
trees.story:
The zelkova a few hundred metres away measures more, but that figure counts four stems grown together. This is one trunk, 6.71 metres round, the thickest single trunk the register records in Landbohøjskolens Have, and it carries a crown 25.7 metres up behind the old auditorium VII.

The garden was inaugurated in 1858 for the Royal Veterinary and Agricultural College, and the university's own history of the place says plainly that trees planted then are still standing, more than 150 years on. It names zelkovas, a golden weeping ash, collections of ash and chestnut. It does not name this plane, so the tree itself rests on the register, which checked its position in 2011 and recorded it healthy and single-stemmed.

Platanus x acerifolia is a hybrid of the oriental plane and the American one, and it became the standard street tree of industrial Europe because it tolerates polluted air and shrugs off root compaction. Most of the ones you meet are pollarded to a fist of knuckles. This one was left to grow, which is why it is worth the walk: a plane allowed to become what it wanted to become.

The garden is free and open, ten minutes on foot from Fasanvej metro.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the single trunk, 6.71 metres round, with the flaking cream and olive bark of a plane. It stands behind the former auditorium VII, and unlike the garden's zelkova it is one stem, not four.

trees.name: The Zelkova of Landbohojskolens Have

location.address: Landbohojskolens Have, about 50 metres south of the garden's northeastern corner

verified_sources: University of Copenhagen's own history of the garden's old trees, which specifically describes large zelkovas along Bulowsvej where several trunks have grown together into one crown, matching this tree's own record of four fused stems: https://kub.ku.dk/biblioteker/frederiksberg/landbohoejskolens-historie/life150/haven/de_gamle_trer/
trees.access: Free, open public garden (Landbohojskolens Have), part of the University of Copenhagen's Frederiksberg Campus.
trees.transport: Fasanvej station (Copenhagen Metro, M1/M2), about 10 minutes on foot.
trees.verify_notes: The register notes the tree consists of 4 stems, with fungal infection at the southeast stem; 755 cm is therefore a multi-stem/crown measurement rather than a single trunk, matching the university source's description of zelkovas here whose several trunks fused into one crown when multiple saplings were planted together, a known 19th-century planting practice at this garden.
trees.story:
This is not one tree with four stems. It is four trees that grew into each other. The university's history of Landbohøjskolens Have describes the zelkovas along Bülowsvej whose separate trunks have fused into a single crown, the result of a nineteenth-century habit of dropping several saplings into one planting hole, and the register's entry for this tree records exactly that: four stems, measured together at 7.55 metres, under 17 metres of shared canopy.

So the girth is a group figure, not a trunk. What it describes is better than a trunk anyway, because the four have knitted into one another at the base and the crown above them behaves as one tree.

Zelkova serrata is an elm relative from Japan, Korea and eastern China, with fine-toothed leaves and smooth grey bark that flakes to orange as it ages. The garden's own history counts its zelkovas among the old trees here, which is more than it says about most of what grows in it.

One caution from the survey in June 2022: there is fungal infection in the southeastern stem. On a tree made of four stems that is a slower problem than it would be on one, but it is worth looking at when you stand there.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the base, four trunks fused into one mass measuring 7.55 metres round, under a single spreading crown 17 metres tall. It stands about 50 metres south of the garden's northeastern corner.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Rosenvaenget

location.address: Pavement outside Rosenvaengets Alle 30, at the corner of Rosenvaengets Alle and Saabyesvej, Osterbro

verified_sources: Danske Landskabsarkitekter (the Danish landscape architects' association), a dedicated feature article on this specific tree, 'Mere end et trae - Rosenvaengets platan', describing it as possibly one of Denmark's oldest surviving plane trees, as tall as the surrounding five-storey buildings, and formally protected as a valuable tree within the Rosenvaenget neighbourhood plan: https://www.landskabsarkitekter.dk/Aktuelt/mere-end-et-trae-rosenvaengets-platan/
trees.access: Free, stands on the public pavement; visible and reachable at any time.
trees.transport: Poul Henningsens Plads (Copenhagen Metro, Cityringen M3), about 10 minutes on foot.
trees.verify_notes: Genuinely well-documented by a dedicated feature article, independent of the register. That article states its exact age is not known, nor is it clear how old a London plane can become in this climate, so do not assign an age; the article's own honesty about the uncertainty should carry into the story. Crown reaches over the roof of the nearest apartment building; healthy per the register.
trees.story:
A tree standing on the pavement in Østerbro has grown as tall as the five-storey blocks around it. The Danish landscape architects' association wrote a whole article about this plane, Mere end et træ, and it makes two claims worth repeating: that this may be one of the oldest surviving plane trees in Denmark, and that nobody knows how old it actually is.

The second part is the honest part. The article says plainly that its age is not established, and that it is not even clear how old a London plane can become in this climate, so there is nothing here to date. What is established is the size: 5.78 metres round, 27 metres tall, with the crown reaching over the roof of the apartment building beside it, recorded healthy by the register in 2019.

It is also protected. The Rosenvænget local plan names it as a valuable tree, which in a neighbourhood of this density means the pavement it stands on cannot simply be rearranged around it.

You can stand under it at any hour, which is rare on this list. It is on the public pavement outside Rosenvængets Allé 30, on the corner of Såbyesvej, and if you happen to know when it was planted, that is the one thing missing.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the height, 27 metres, level with the five-storey blocks around it, on a trunk 5.78 metres round standing in the pavement itself. It is on the corner of Rosenvængets Allé and Såbyesvej.

trees.name: The Lanceleaf Cottonwood of Bispebjerg Kirkegard

location.address: Bispebjerg Kirkegard, on the lawn between Nordre and Sondre Kapel, nearest the northern one

verified_sources: Kobenhavns Kommune's own page on Bispebjerg Kirkegard confirming it is open to the public and describing its avenues of poplar, pine, ash, hornbeam and Japanese cherry trees: https://www.kk.dk/brug-byen/natur-og-groenne-omraader/koebenhavns-kirkegaarde/bispebjerg-kirkegaard
trees.access: Free, the cemetery is open to the public in daylight hours.
trees.transport: Norrebro station (S-train), about 20 minutes on foot, or bus 6A/350S to the cemetery gate on Frederikssundsvej.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: the municipal cemetery page confirms poplar avenues exist at Bispebjerg generally and confirms public access, but does not name this specific tree/species, so it stands as context. This individual is the northernmost of a group of three trees; the register's own legend notes some variation in leaf length-to-width ratio within the group and that there is no official Danish name for this poplar species (Populus acuminata is a North American hybrid cottonwood, not native to Denmark). Ask the reader if this identification looks right, since the register itself flags it with question marks in its Danish name field.
trees.story:
The register is not sure what this tree is, and puts question marks in its own name field to say so. It files it as Populus acuminata, a North American hybrid cottonwood with no established Danish name, and the surveyor noted that the leaves within this group of three vary in how long they are against how wide, which is exactly the measurement the identification turns on.

So here it is, published with the doubt attached. It is 2.36 metres round and 20 metres tall, the northernmost of the three, standing on the lawn between the northern and southern chapels of Bispebjerg Kirkegård. If you know poplars and you can settle it, that is a correction we would be glad to make.

The cemetery is worth the trip on its own account. Copenhagen laid it out with avenues of poplar, pine, ash, hornbeam and Japanese cherry, so the planting is not a graveyard's usual scatter of yew and lime but something closer to an arboretum with graves in it. The city's own description of the place leads with the trees.

Only the register names this individual. Everything above about the tree itself comes from one survey in July 2017.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its place in the line: the northernmost of three poplars on the lawn between the two chapels, 20 metres tall on a trunk 2.36 metres round, with long narrow poplar leaves.
