trees.name: The Catalpa of Haveselskabets Have

location.address: Haveselskabets Have, Frederiksberg, just inside the entrance

verified_sources: Visit Copenhagen's own listing for Haveselskabets Have, confirming it as a free public park in Frederiksberg, open year-round: https://www.visitcopenhagen.com/copenhagen/planning/haveselskabets-have-gdk1137394
trees.access: Free, open public park (Haveselskabets Have, run by the Danish Horticultural Society), open year-round, roughly 06:00 to 17:00-22:00 depending on the season.
trees.transport: Frederiksberg Alle station (Copenhagen Metro, M1/M2), a couple of minutes on foot.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: the Visit Copenhagen source confirms the park and its public access but does not name this specific catalpa, so it stands as access context. Forked from about 2 metres up per the register's legend. Healthy, single main stem below the fork.
trees.story:
The catalpa is among the last trees in any garden to come into leaf, so for several weeks each spring it stands there looking dead while everything around it is green. Then it produces leaves the size of a hand, white foxglove-shaped flowers in midsummer, and long thin seed pods that hang on through the winter.

This one is just inside the entrance of Haveselskabets Have, the Danish Horticultural Society's garden in Frederiksberg, 2.17 metres round and 12 metres tall. It forks about two metres up and continues as a pair of limbs, which is the ordinary way a southern catalpa builds itself: wide rather than high, more umbrella than column.

The garden is free and open all year, roughly from six in the morning until somewhere between five and ten at night depending on the season, which makes this one of the easier trees on this list to get to. It is a couple of minutes from Frederiksberg Allé metro.

Only the register names the tree. The garden is well documented and this catalpa is not, beyond a survey in September 2023 that measured it and recorded it healthy. Nobody has dated it, and no age is guessed at here.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the huge heart-shaped leaves and the long thin seed pods hanging from the crown, on a trunk that forks in two about two metres up. It stands just inside the garden entrance.

trees.name: The Tulip Tree of J.C. Jacobsens Have

location.address: J.C. Jacobsens Have, Carlsberg Byen, on the western lawn toward the northwest

verified_sources: Carlsberg Byen's own account of J.C. Jacobsens Have as J.C. Jacobsen's historic private tree collection, opened to the public in 2009: https://www.carlsbergbyen.dk/om-carlsberg-byen/byrum-i-carlsberg-byen/jc-jacobsens-have
trees.access: Free, open public park (J.C. Jacobsens Have), part of Carlsberg Byen.
trees.transport: Carlsberg station (S-train), about 10 minutes on foot.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: as with the garden's other Carlsberg trees, the second source confirms the garden's general history but not this specific tulip tree by name. Single-stemmed, healthy (Levende, sund). At 26.5 m one of the taller trees in this batch, notable for the tulip-shaped flowers in early summer, though no source here confirms bloom timing for this specimen so best_time is left unset.
trees.story:
The flowers this tree is named for open in June, high in the crown, and most people standing under it never see one. Liriodendron tulipifera carries greenish orange blooms shaped like tulips, and it carries them at the top, twenty metres up in this case, which is why the ground under an old tulip tree in summer is often the only place you find them.

This is one of the tallest trees in J.C. Jacobsens Have at 26.5 metres, on a single stem 3.92 metres round, standing on the western lawn toward the northwest. The garden was the private ground of the brewer who founded Carlsberg, laid out in 1848 and stocked with trees he brought back from his travels; it opened to the public in 2009. The Carlsberg account tells that story about the garden and not about this tree, so the tulip tree itself rests on the register survey of April 2019, which recorded it healthy.

The leaf is the other oddity. It looks like a maple leaf with the tip cut off square, unmistakable once you have seen one, and in late October the whole crown of them turns clear yellow.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, shaped as though the tip had been cut off square, on a single trunk 3.92 metres round under a crown 26.5 metres tall. It stands on the western lawn toward the northwest.

best_time.label: late October, when the whole crown turns clear yellow

trees.name: Fortunegen, the Fortune Oak of Dyrehaven

location.address: Jaegersborg Dyrehave (the royal deer park), Lyngby-Taarbaek Kommune, east of Fortunporthuset gatehouse, north of Fortunvej

trees.access: Free, open daily; Jaegersborg Dyrehave is a public royal deer park.
trees.transport: Jaegersborg station (Naerumbanen), then about a 10-15 minute walk to the Fortunporten gate, which is much closer than Klampenborg for this particular oak on the park's western side.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: register-only, no independent second source found; the hiking blog used for Trepileegen/Kuppelegen/Vorteegen does not mention Fortunegen. Named for its position near Fortunporten, one of the deer park's historic gates. Crown very asymmetric, squeezed on the north side, per the register's legend. Age DERIVED from girth 580 cm (diameter about 185 cm) using the open-grown oak multiplier of roughly 1.25-2.0 years/cm, giving approximately 230-370 years, notably younger than the four other named Dyrehaven oaks in this batch, consistent with its smaller girth.
trees.story:
The crown of this oak is lopsided. The surveyor recorded it as strongly asymmetric, squeezed flat on the north side and full on the south, which is what happens to a tree that spent its life with something crowding it from one direction.

It is also the junior of Dyrehaven's named oaks on this list. At 5.80 metres round it is nearly three metres slimmer than Trepileegen, and the arithmetic reflects that: a trunk of about 1.85 metres across, at the growth rates an open-grown oak manages, works out at somewhere between roughly 225 and 375 years. That is derived from the girth rather than measured on the tree, and it still makes this oak older than almost anything standing in central Copenhagen.

Fortunegen takes its name from Fortunporten, one of the deer park's old gates, and it stands east of the Fortunporthuset gatehouse just north of Fortunvej. That corner of the park has its own station: Jægersborg on the Nærumbanen is ten to fifteen minutes away on foot, where the other oaks here mean a walk of half an hour or more from Klampenborg.

Only the register carries this one. The walking account that names the park's other giants does not mention it at all.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, flattened on the north side and full on the south, over a trunk 5.80 metres round, slimmer than the park's other named oaks. It stands east of the Fortunporthuset gatehouse.

trees.name: The Black Locust of Lindevangsparken

location.address: Lindevangsparken, southeastern corner, Frederiksberg

trees.access: Free, open public park (Lindevangsparken).
trees.transport: Peter Bangs Vej station (Copenhagen Metro, M1/M2), about 5-10 minutes on foot.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: register-only, no independent second source found for this individual tree. Large bark wound on the south side per the register's legend. Single-stemmed.
trees.story:
Something took a large piece of bark off the south side of this tree and it carried on growing. The wound is the first thing the register records about it after the measurements, and the measurements are 2.92 metres round and 21.5 metres tall, on one stem, in the southeastern corner of Lindevangsparken.

That height is the interesting part. Robinia pseudoacacia is an American tree, from the Appalachians, planted across Europe for centuries because its timber resists rot in the ground, and in a park it often ends up as a leaning, suckering, many-stemmed thing. This one went straight up instead and kept a single trunk while doing it.

The giveaways are all at eye level and above: bark furrowed into deep ropes, pairs of short spines at the base of the twigs, leaves divided into rows of small oval leaflets, and hanging clusters of white pea flowers in early summer that smell strongly enough to find the tree by.

Only the register carries it. The position and condition were checked in June 2023, the tree was recorded alive, and nobody has dated it, so no age is offered here. Lindevangsparken is free and open, five to ten minutes from Peter Bangs Vej metro.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the deeply ridged bark, the paired spines on the twigs and the rows of small oval leaflets, on a single trunk 2.92 metres round with a large wound on its south side.

trees.name: The Cherry Avenue of Bispebjerg Kirkegard

location.address: Bispebjerg Kirkegard, the cherry avenue (Kirsebaeralleen)

verified_sources: Kristeligt Dagblad, reporting that thousands visit the cherry avenue at Bispebjerg each spring: https://www.kristeligt-dagblad.dk/bagsiden/tusinder-besoeger-kirsebaeralleen-paa-bispebjerg

TV 2 Kosmopol, reporting the avenue drew an expected 150,000 visitors during its 2026 bloom: https://www.tv2kosmopol.dk/koebenhavn/se-billederne-kirsebaertraeer-blomstrer-paa-bispebjerg-forventer-150000-besoegende

migogkbh.dk, which gives the avenue's planting history: replaced in 1992 an earlier elm avenue lost to Dutch elm disease, and today comprises around 43 Prunus 'Accolade' trees: https://migogkbh.dk/nu-springer-kirsebaeralleen-ud/
trees.access: Free, the cemetery is open to the public in daylight hours; the avenue draws very large crowds during its bloom and is best visited outside peak bloom weekends if a quiet walk is wanted.
trees.transport: Norrebro station (S-train), about 20 minutes on foot, or bus 6A/350S to the cemetery gate on Frederikssundsvej.
trees.verify_notes: SHIPS AS AN ENSEMBLE, not a single trunk: about 43 Prunus 'Accolade' trees planted together in 1992 as a formal avenue, replacing an earlier elm avenue killed by Dutch elm disease. This passes the compact-famous-ensemble test: it is a single continuous avenue with one obvious place to stand (walking its length), it is famous specifically for being exactly this (an avenue, not individual trees), and it draws well-documented crowds (100,000-150,000 visitors during peak bloom weeks per press). No trunk girth or height applies to an avenue entry; do not invent one. Ornamental cultivar, does not fruit. Blooms normally in the second half of April per the register; press sources say mid-April. best_time set to April flowering.
trees.story:
Around 150,000 people were expected to walk this avenue during a fortnight of bloom in 2026. It is a cemetery path, and for two weeks a year it is one of the busiest places in Copenhagen.

Be clear about what it is. The cherries went in in 1992, about 43 of them, replacing an avenue of elms that Dutch elm disease had killed. So this is not an ancient tree and it is not really a tree at all: it is an avenue, and the avenue is the destination. You walk the length of it under a continuous roof of pink, which is a different thing from standing in front of one old trunk, and it is why the entry exists.

The cultivar is Prunus 'Accolade', an ornamental that flowers hard and sets no useful fruit. The register puts the bloom in the second half of April, the press usually reports it in the middle of the month, and the truth is that it moves with the year and lasts around two weeks.

Bispebjerg Kirkegård is a working burial ground with people being buried in it. On peak weekends the avenue is crowded to the point of queueing, so early mornings and weekdays are the way to walk it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it at once: the single straight avenue of some 43 cherries inside Bispebjerg Kirkegård, arching over the path from both sides. No other planting in the cemetery runs as one continuous line of pink.

best_time.label: the second half of April, when the whole avenue flowers at once

trees.name: The Caucasian Oak of Vestre Kirkegard

location.address: Vestre Kirkegard, section I (afsnit I)

verified_sources: Wonderful Copenhagen's cemetery map and guide to Vestre Kirkegard's selected graves and botany, marking this tree as tree number 2 on its own overview map, an independent published guide to the cemetery's notable specimens: https://wonderfulcphdotcom.files.wordpress.com/2013/10/kort-over-vestre-kirkegaard-1.pdf

Kobenhavns Kommune's own page on Vestre Kirkegard, confirming it is open to the public year-round (07:00-19:00 in winter, 07:00-22:00 in summer) and welcomes recreational use: https://www.kk.dk/brug-byen/byens-groenne-oaser/koebenhavns-kirkegaarde/vestre-kirkegaard
trees.access: Free, the cemetery is open to the public daily, 07:00-19:00 in winter (October-March) and 07:00-22:00 in summer (April-September).
trees.transport: Sjaelor station (S-train), a short walk along the cemetery's southern edge, or Valby station a little further to the north-west.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED on the measurement, not on existence: the register's headline girth is 2.98 m, but its own legend notes the tree is grafted onto a pedunculate oak rootstock and has a number of epicormic growth pads (vanrispuder) low on the trunk, which push the circumference at 1.3 m height to about 4.0 m at that irregular point. 298 cm is used here as the more representative clear-trunk figure; say in the story that the true grafted union is thicker and knobbly. Named tree number 2 on Wonderful Copenhagen's own botanical map of the cemetery, a genuinely independent guide.
trees.story:
Measure this oak at chest height, where the tape is supposed to go, and you get about four metres. Measure it where the trunk is clean and you get 2.98. Both figures sit in the same register entry and neither is wrong.

The reason is that it is a grafted tree. A Caucasian oak has been grafted onto a pedunculate oak rootstock, and low on the trunk it carries pads of epicormic growth, the knobbly clusters of small shoots that a graft often throws, which swell the circumference exactly where the measurement is meant to be taken. The 2.98 metres used here is the honest clear-trunk figure. What you will see is thicker than that and lumpy with it.

Above the join it is straightforwardly a Quercus macranthera, an oak from the Caucasus and northern Iran with large, deeply lobed leaves and downy young shoots, standing 20.5 metres tall in section I of Vestre Kirkegård.

Somebody besides the register thought it worth pointing at: Wonderful Copenhagen's own map of the cemetery marks it as tree number two on a walking guide to the place. The cemetery is free and open daily, from seven in the morning until seven in winter and ten in summer.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the base, knobbly with clusters of small shoots where it was grafted, swelling to about four metres round above a clear trunk of 2.98. It is tree number two on the cemetery's own map, in section I.

trees.name: The Service Tree of J.C. Jacobsens Have

location.address: J.C. Jacobsens Have, Carlsberg Byen, 40 metres due north of the fountain

verified_sources: Carlsberg Byen's own account of J.C. Jacobsens Have as J.C. Jacobsen's historic tree collection, opened to the public in 2009: https://www.carlsbergbyen.dk/om-carlsberg-byen/byrum-i-carlsberg-byen/jc-jacobsens-have
trees.access: Free, open public park (J.C. Jacobsens Have), part of Carlsberg Byen.
trees.transport: Carlsberg station (S-train), about 10 minutes on foot.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: as with the garden's other Carlsberg trees, the second source confirms the garden's general history but not this specific tree by name. Service tree (Sorbus domestica) is a genuine rarity in Denmark, a wild relative of the rowan that bears small pear- or apple-shaped fruit; the register's own legend simply calls it 'a large and beautiful tree'. Single-stemmed, healthy.
trees.story:
The register's surveyors deal in centimetres and growth forms. For this one the note says simply that it is a large and beautiful tree, and stops there.

The reason for the lapse is probably the species. Sorbus domestica, the service tree, is a genuine rarity in Denmark: a wild relative of the rowan that grows slowly, fruits sparsely, and turns up in old collections rather than in parks. The fruit is the tell, small and shaped like a miniature pear or apple rather than the rowan's cluster of red berries, and it was once gathered and left to go soft before anybody would eat it.

This one is 3.18 metres round and 16 metres tall on a single stem, standing 40 metres due north of the fountain in J.C. Jacobsens Have, and the register recorded it healthy in April 2019. The garden was laid out in 1848 as the private grounds of the brewer who founded Carlsberg and filled over the years with trees he brought home from his travels; it opened to the public in 2009. Whether this service tree was one of his is not recorded, so the tree itself stands on the register entry alone.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the rowan-like leaves, many leaflets to a stalk, over small pear-shaped fruit rather than red berries, on a single trunk 3.18 metres round. It stands 40 metres due north of the fountain.

trees.name: The Hungarian Oak of Bispebjerg Kirkegard

location.address: Bispebjerg Kirkegard, about 90 metres northwest of Nordre Kapel

verified_sources: Kobenhavns Kommune's own page on Bispebjerg Kirkegard, confirming public access and the cemetery's varied tree avenues: https://www.kk.dk/brug-byen/natur-og-groenne-omraader/koebenhavns-kirkegaarde/bispebjerg-kirkegaard
trees.access: Free, the cemetery is open to the public in daylight hours.
trees.transport: Norrebro station (S-train), about 20 minutes on foot, or bus 6A/350S to the cemetery gate on Frederikssundsvej.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: the municipal cemetery page confirms general access but does not name this specific oak. Free-standing with a full, healthy crown per the register's legend (fritstaende og fuldkronet, sund). A different species from the register's several Pedunculate Oaks in this batch; Quercus frainetto is native to southeastern Europe, not Denmark, so this is a planted ornamental rather than a native survivor.
trees.story:
This oak is a long way from home. Quercus frainetto grows wild in southeastern Europe, in the Balkans and down into southern Italy, so nothing about it is a Danish survivor: somebody planted it here on purpose, and it has done well enough to reach 4.19 metres round and 23.5 metres tall.

The register describes it as free-standing and full-crowned, which in a cemetery means it has had the space and the light to build the shape it wanted, without competition on any side. It stands about 90 metres northwest of Nordre Kapel at Bispebjerg Kirkegård, where the city planted whole avenues of poplar, pine, ash, hornbeam and Japanese cherry and ended up with something closer to a collection than a churchyard.

The leaves settle the identification on the spot. Hungarian oak carries the largest leaves of any European oak, deeply cut into many lobes and crowded toward the ends of the shoots, so the crown looks heavier and darker than a Danish oak's from a distance.

Only the register names the tree. The city's cemetery page confirms the avenues and the public access and says nothing about this individual, and nobody has dated it, so no age is offered here.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, much larger than a Danish oak's and cut into many lobes, crowded at the shoot tips, on a free-standing trunk 4.19 metres round. It stands about 90 metres northwest of Nordre Kapel.
